caption: The benchmark table: every test of hazbrief against a published result
definitions_heading: Definitions: what the benchmark table's rows, columns and names mean

definitions.text: one test of hazbrief against a published result. BENCH-0 is the requirement the others serve: as a minimum, hazbrief does as well as each accepted tool; as its objective, better (its state is note 5).

columns.name: Test
columns.text: the benchmark row's id and a plain name for it.

columns.name: Run
columns.text: the model run being compared (the names are below); empty where no run is held.

columns.name: Compared with
columns.text: the trial's measurements, or a tool's published run of the same trial (why these tools: note 3).

columns.name: Arcs (n)
columns.text: how many sampling arcs, at fixed distances from the release, are compared; each arc gives its maximum concentration.

columns.name: Ratio
columns.text: against the measurements, the geometric mean of measured over predicted concentration (MG); against a tool, the run's MG divided by the tool's. 1 means no difference; above 1 means the run's concentrations are lower.

columns.name: 95 percent limits
columns.text: the range the ratio could plausibly be in, at the 95 percent confidence level (the method: note 2).

columns.name: Within a factor of two (k of n)
columns.text: how many arcs' predicted maximum is within a factor of two of the measured one; a count, not a test.

columns.name: Statistically different?
columns.text: Yes when the 95 percent limits leave out 1, with below or above for the run's concentrations; No when they include 1; Not yet tested where no run is held.

columns.name: Note
columns.text: the numbers of the notes below the table that bear on the row.

names.text: hazbrief's run of SCICHEM, the puff model that draws a dense release's cloud on the brief.
hazbrief's run of SLAB, the dense-gas model (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, 1990), at 20 or 80 percent relative humidity.
HPAC's two published runs of the trial: with a complex source (the 17-model comparison) and a simple jet-only source (Simpson et al. 2020).
ALOHA's (Areal Locations of Hazardous Atmospheres) published run of the trial in the 17-model comparison.

notes: Jack Rabbit II Trial 7: one trial, five arcs at 0.2 to 5 km, all of one release, not five independent releases.
The limits are Hanna, Strimaitis and Chang (1993), equation 34, at the 95 percent confidence level; the words are the Census Bureau's.
Why HPAC and ALOHA, the operator: "the community tools that people have been relying on ... the gold standard for the community."
Two models can agree and both be wrong (Warner et al., page 40). The operator: "they can still be useful for making decisions."
BENCH-0's minimum, doing as well as each tool: not statistically significant at 95 percent against HPAC or ALOHA (one trial, five arcs).
